units.text: INT. GHOSTS - CONTINUOUS

Well, I seem to find explanation and confirmation of all sorts of things I myself have been thinking. For that is the wonderful part of it, Pastor Manders--there is really nothing new in these books, nothing but what most people think and believe. Only most people either don't formulate it to themselves, or else keep quiet about it.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Great heavens! Do you really believe that most people--?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: I do, indeed.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: But surely not in this country? Not here among us?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Yes, certainly; here as elsewhere.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Well, I really must say--!
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: For the rest, what do you object to in these books?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Object to in them? You surely do not suppose that I have nothing better to do than to study such publications as these?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: That is to say, you know nothing of what you are condemning?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: I have read enough about these writings to disapprove of them.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Yes; but your own judgment--
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: My dear Mrs. Alving, there are many occasions in life when one must rely upon others. Things are so ordered in this world; and it is well that they are. Otherwise, what would become of society?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Well, well, I daresay you're right there.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Besides, I of course do not deny that there may be much that is attractive in such books. Nor can I blame you for wishing to keep up with the intellectual movements that are said to be going on in the great world-where you have let your son pass so much of his life. But--
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: But?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Lowering his voice.
But one should not talk about it, Mrs. Alving. One is certainly not bound to account to everybody for what one reads and thinks within one's own four walls.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Of course not; I quite agree with you.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Only think, now, how you are bound to consider the interests of this Orphanage, which you decided on founding at a time when--if I understand you rightly--you thought very differently on spiritual matters.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Oh, yes; I quite admit that. But it was about the Orphanage--
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: It was about the Orphanage we were to speak; yes. All I say is: prudence, my dear lady! And now let us get to business.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Opens the packet, and takes out a number of papers.
Do you see these?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: The documents?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: All--and in perfect order. I can tell you it was hard work to get them in time. I had to put on strong pressure. The authorities are almost morbidly scrupulous when there is any decisive step to be taken. But here they are at last.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Looks through the bundle.

See! here is the formal deed of gift of the parcel of ground known as Solvik in the Manor of Rosenvold, with all the newly constructed buildings, schoolrooms, master's house, and chapel. And here is the legal fiat for the endowment and for the Bye-laws of the Institution. Will you look at them?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Reads.
"Bye-laws for the Children's Home to be known as 'Captain Alving's Foundation.'"
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: (Looks long at the paper.) So there it is.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: I have chosen the designation "Captain" rather than "Chamberlain." "Captain" looks less pretentious.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Oh, yes; just as you think best.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: And here you have the Bank Account of the capital lying at interest to cover the current expenses of the Orphanage.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Thank you; but please keep it--it will be more convenient.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: With pleasure. I think we will leave the money in the Bank for the present. The interest is certainly not what we could wish--four per cent. and six months' notice of withdrawal. If a good mortgage could be found later on--of course it must be a first mortgage and an unimpeachable security--then we could consider the matter.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Certainly, my dear Pastor Manders. You are the best judge in these things.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: I will keep my eyes open at any rate.--But now there is one thing more which I have several times been intending to ask you.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: And what is that?
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Shall the Orphanage buildings be insured or not?
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Of course they must be insured.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Well, wait a moment, Mrs. Alving. Let us look into the matter a little more closely.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: I have everything insured; buildings and movables and stock and crops.
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: Of course you have--on your own estate. And so have I--of course. But here, you see, it is quite another matter. The Orphanage is to be consecrated, as it were, to a higher purpose.
units.name: MANDERS

units.text: Yes, but that's no reason--
units.name: MRS. ALVING

units.text: For my own part, I should certainly not see the smallest impropriety in guarding against all contingencies--
units.name: MANDERS
